jobs.name: Garden wall
jobs.brief: Garden wall in stretcher bond: six bricks long, eight courses high, on the concrete footing. Keep every brick on the string line.

afterCourse.0: Course done. 71 mm brick + 12.3 mm bed joint = 83.3 mm per course, so twelve courses make exactly one metre. Next course starts with a half brick, so no vertical joint sits on top of the one below. That's stretcher bond.
afterCourse.3: Halfway. On a real site you'd also hold the spirit level upright against the wall to check it is plumb.

jobs.name: Corner
jobs.brief: Corner job: two walls meeting at 90°, six courses. Corners first: every course starts with the corner brick, because it sets the line for both walls. Hot afternoon, so the mortar stiffens faster. Once your two lead courses are down, you can hand the rest to the robot.

afterCourse.0: Now the courses swap: this time the corner brick runs along the other wall. Alternating like this keeps the half-brick overlap on both walls without cutting a single brick.
afterCourse.2: Halfway up. A real bricklayer builds the corners several courses ahead of the rest of the wall, stepping each course back by half a brick. That's called racking back.

jobs.name: Yard walls
jobs.brief: Yard walls: three walls around a small yard. Lay the first two courses of each wall yourself, since they set the line and the bond. Then hand the wall to the robot (H) and move on to the next one.

afterCourse.1: Lead done. On real sites the best bricklayer sets out the first courses and the corners, and the walling in between goes faster. Press H to hand this wall to the robot and move on.

jobs.name: Window wall
jobs.brief: Window wall: eight bricks long, twelve courses high, with a window opening in the middle. Lay the first two courses yourself, then hand over. The robot leaves the gap open and closes each reveal with a half brick every other course. The lintel over the gap is yours to set: the robot will call you.

afterCourse.1: Lead done, and you're at sill height. From the next course up the window gap stays open. Press H to hand the wall to the robot.
afterCourse.7: The opening is at full height. Next course: the precast lintel across the gap. The robot stops here and calls you over.

upgrades.name: Bigger trowel
upgrades.desc: One load of mortar beds three bricks instead of two.

upgrades.name: Mortar retarder
upgrades.desc: An admixture that keeps mortar workable 50% longer. Real sites use it on hot days.

upgrades.name: Brick tongs
upgrades.desc: Carry two bricks per trip from the pallet.

upgrades.name: Apprentice
upgrades.desc: Hands you the next brick every time you lay one.

upgrades.name: Robot: faster arm
upgrades.desc: The robot lays a brick every 0.8 s instead of 1.6 s.

clipboard.spread: Spread a mortar bed on the glowing spot
clipboard.scrape: The mortar has gone off. Scrape it away and spread fresh
clipboard.grab-full: Take a brick from the pallet
clipboard.grab-half: This spot needs a half brick. Take one from the small stack
clipboard.swap: Wrong size. Swap it at the stack
clipboard.place: Lay the brick on the mortar bed
clipboard.hit: Level it to the line: aim at the high end. Click = light tap, hold = firm knock
clipboard.done: Job finished. Stand back and admire it
clipboard.watch: The robot is finishing the walls. Watch it work, or walk around
clipboard.handover: Lead done: hand this wall to the robot (H) or keep laying
clipboard.grab-lintel: This spot needs the lintel. Take one from the lintel stack
clipboard.lintelCall: The robot has reached the lintel course and stopped. Set the lintel over the window gap yourself

facts.firstLoad: Mortar is roughly 1 part cement to 4 parts sand, mixed stiff and buttery. It starts to stiffen as soon as it's spread, so only spread what you can lay.
facts.firstPlace: That's an NF brick: 240 × 115 × 71 mm, about 3 kg. It landed tilted, so tap the high end first. Both ends have to finish on the string line.
facts.firstSet: On the line. The mortar under it, the bed joint, ends up about 12 mm thick.
facts.firstSunk: Too low: you squeezed out too much mortar. Lift it and lay it again. Light taps near the line, firm knocks only when it sits high.
facts.mortarOff: The mortar has gone off: it's too stiff to bed a brick properly. Scrape it back and spread fresh. Never lay onto stiff mortar, because the brick won't bond.
facts.streak: Four perfect in a row: your pay goes up while the streak lasts. One sloppy brick resets it.
facts.proud: The mortar went off before that brick reached the line, so it's stuck proud. Knock high bricks hard and fast, then finish with light taps.
facts.robot: From now on the bricklaying robot works with you. Lay the first two courses of a wall yourself, then hand it over and move on. Machines like this really exist: some lay around 3,000 bricks a day beside a human bricklayer.
facts.reveal: That's a reveal, the side of the opening. Every other course ends at the gap with a half brick, so the bond carries on right up to the edge and the reveal stays straight.
facts.lintel: A clay-shell lintel (Flachsturz) must bear at least 115 mm on the brickwork each side. This one is 0.99 m long over a 0.51 m gap, so it sits 240 mm, a full brick, on each side.
facts.overLintel: The lintel on its own is weak. It gets its strength from the brickwork laid on top of it, which works as the compression zone, so the courses above count as part of the lintel.

garden: One course is 83.3 mm, so 12 courses = 1 m.
Stretcher bond offsets each course by half a brick.
Mortar stiffens once it's spread, so only spread what you can lay.
corner: Corners are built first; they set the line for both walls.
At a corner the courses alternate direction, which keeps the bond without cutting bricks.
Heat and wind make mortar stiffen faster; retarders slow it down.
Building the corners ahead, stepped back half a brick per course, is called racking back.
yard: The first courses set the line and the bond for the whole wall, so the most skilled hands lay them.
Bricklaying robots handle the repetitive walling, and a human still sets out and checks the work.
Splitting a job into sections lets a crew work on several walls at once.
Stretcher bond works the same on every wall: half-brick overlap, 10 mm head joints.
window: Openings are sized in the brick grid: two bricks left out plus their joints make a 0.51 m gap.
At a reveal every other course ends with a half brick, so the bond carries on to the edge.
A clay-shell lintel needs at least 115 mm of bearing each side; this one gets a full brick, 240 mm.
A clay lintel works together with the brickwork above it: the courses on top are part of the lintel.
